abstract: This paper presents a concept and implementation of AI-enabled Multi-Agent Systems in service-oriented manufacturing networks. Building on the Asset Administration Shell as a standardized digital representation of assets, product and resource agents were designed to coordinate production processes autonomously, while AI-powered service agents provided additional reasoning capabilities. The approach was validated in a testbed through the production of a customized Multi-Key-Tool. The results show that AI-powered Multi-Agent Systems enable semantic interoperability, decentralized orchestration of processes, and adaptation to customer-specific requirements. At the same time, challenges remain regarding standardized discovery of agents and their assets, cross-company methods, and efficient AI reasoning in real-time shopfloor contexts.
title: Learnings from implementing AI Agents in Service-Oriented Manufacturing Ecosystems using Fetch.ai

abstract: ABSTRACT The transition from Industry 4.0 to the value‐driven human‐centric Industry 5.0 paradigm increasingly relies on autonomous AI agents for complex decision‐making. However, existing research remains fragmented within isolated operational silos. This systematic review aims to unify this landscape by analysing the deployment of agentic architectures encompassing classical multiagent systems, deep reinforcement learning and large language models (LLMs) across production scheduling, maintenance management and supply chain optimisation. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically analysed 118 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026. The findings reveal a critical maturity asymmetry: although agentic methods are highly advanced in diagnostic monitoring and localised execution, a structural ‘deployment gap’ persists at the real‐time prescriptive decision‐making step across all three domains. This bottleneck is primarily driven by unresolved vulnerabilities in algorithmic explainability, safety verification and cybersecurity. As a central novelty, this review introduces a cross‐domain taxonomy that categorises agent architectures and synthesises their shared cyber‐physical dependencies, including digital twins, edge‐distributed computing and semantic interoperability standards. By evaluating these traditionally isolated literature together, we expose performance discrepancies where identical architectures yield markedly different outcomes depending on the operational context. Finally, we propose a comprehensive research roadmap to bridge the deployment gap, emphasising the need for robust explainable AI (XAI), federated learning for cross‐organisational data governance and sociotechnical frameworks that ensure genuine human–agent collaboration. Ultimately, closing this gap is essential for realising the fully self‐organising resilient industrial networks envisioned by Industry 5.0.
title: Autonomous AI Agents in Industrial Operations: A Systematic Review of Production Scheduling, Predictive Maintenance and Supply Chain Optimisation

abstract: The evolution of autonomous multi-agent systems has created an urgent need for standardized, interoperable communication protocols capable of orchestrating complex, stateful workflows across heterogeneous agents. Traditional point-topoint (P2P) API designs and monolithic orchestration platforms lack the modularity, extensibility, and observability required to scale dynamic, decentralized agent ecosystems. The Agentto-Agent (A2A) protocol emerges as a foundational solution by leveraging HTTP, JavaScript Object Notation-Remote Procedure Call (JSON-RPC), and Server-Sent Events (SSE) to enable discoverable capabilities, task-driven workflows, structured artifact exchanges, and real-time status updates. This review article provides a comprehensive analysis of the A2A protocol, articulating its core architectural principles-including the role of Agent Cards, Tasks, Messages, Parts, and Artifacts-as well as the transport, authentication, and event-driven mechanisms that underpin secure and auditable agent interoperability. We examine a broad range of industrial and research use cases, spanning enterprise automation, smart manufacturing, supply chain orchestration, personalized education, and disaster management. Furthermore, we critically evaluate deployment challenges such as schema evolution, multi-tenant authentication, durable state persistence, semantic interoperability, and privacy preservation. Drawing from these insights, we propose prescriptive design patterns and best practices to ensure robust, scalable A2A system implementations. Finally, we highlight future research directions, including decentralized discovery, confidential computing, and AI-driven orchestration, positioning A2A as a keystone for building resilient, composable agentic networks across domains.
title: A Review on Agent-to-Agent Protocol: Concept, State-of-the-art, Challenges and Future Directions

abstract: The industrial deployment of LLM-driven autonomous agents faces an essential contradiction: human natural language is ambiguous, context-dependent and pragmatic, while large language models are token-probability symbolic machines without real-world semantic grounding. Combined with the Long-Chain Reasoning Drift (LCRD) hypothesis elaborated in the author’s parallel independent working paper (see Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21790132), this fundamental mismatch inevitably induces systematic reasoning deviation in multi-step task execution, including hallucinations, logical breaks and untraceable agent behaviors. Taking the LCRD hypothesis as its core theoretical premise, this paper derives a structural formal intermediate layer based on UML to realize controllable industrial agent architectures. From the first principles of the Symbol Grounding Problem, this paper deduces that controllable and auditable agents cannot be achieved by simply enhancing the language comprehension ability of LLMs. Instead, a formal intermediate layer must be inserted between human intention and model execution. We argue that Unified Modeling Language (UML) uniquely meets the dual requirements of human readability/auditability and stable symbolic execution without reasoning drift. A closed-loop pipeline is proposed: LLM generation of UML diagrams → human review and revision of UML → rigid LLM execution guided by UML → error backtracking to UML layer. The paradigm cannot completely eliminate hallucinations, yet it drastically suppresses long-chain drift and delivers industrially viable, fully traceable autonomous agents. Existing agent frameworks including LangGraph, CrewAI and AutoGen partially adopt graph-based constraints but leave three unclosed structural gaps: automated graph generation, formal graph verification, and iterative graph updating. Our first-principle-based architecture naturally resolves all three gaps and can be fully implemented with off-the-shelf LLM APIs and diagramming tools without future technological breakthroughs.
title: UML as a Formal Boundary: A Controllable Middle-Layer Paradigm for AI Agents for AI Agents Based on Symbol Grounding Theory
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) have extended beyond the original concept of a static digital model, to a dynamic, data-driven, and increasingly intelligent cyber-physical structure, which underlies modern Industry 4.0 systems. The paper gives a comprehensive and integrative conceptualization of DTs, Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs), and agentic AI-enhanced DTs through an organized narrative literature review which synthesizes the foundational definitions, the theoretical differences between DTs and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS), and the evolution of Digital Models and Digital Shadows to fully synchronous, two-way DTs. The research synthesizes the major architectural models, such as layered, multi-dimensional, cognitive and agentic models, and discusses the facilitating technologies that enable real-time synchronization, semantic reasoning, and autonomous decision-making. The state-of-the-art analysis indicates that the key research trends include ecosystem-based DTs, AI-driven analytics, semantic enrichment, and the development of LLM-enabled agentic DTs that are able to plan and coordinate actions in a goal-oriented manner. The paper also compares industrial and open-source DT platforms, outlines the present-day limitations in semantic interoperability, cognitive integration, and autonomy and demonstrates real-world applications in manufacturing, healthcare, smart cities, and energy systems. The discussion proposes future research directions such as standardized cognitive layers, safe LLM grounding, multi-DT coordination, and governance frameworks of autonomous DT ecosystems. Overall, the paper contributes a unified conceptual model and a holistic synthesis that connects theory, architecture, technology, and application, providing a foundation for advancing the next generation of intelligent Digital Twin systems.
title: Conceptualizing Cognitive and Agentic Digital Twins
venue: International Multidisciplinary Journal of Emerging Technologies and Applications

abstract: Engineering design currently requires professionals to translate conceptual intent into software-specific representations such as CAD drawings and Building Information Models, making mastery of modelling standards and complex authoring tools a substantial part of engineering work. This paper asks whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can separate engineering semantics from software-specific syntax by serving as a natural-language interface while generating deterministic representations for existing engineering software. We propose a modular agentic architecture based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and validate it through two implementations, BIMCP for Autodesk Revit and BONCP for Blender Bonsai/IFC (Industry Foundation Classes), in which LLMs generate and execute deterministic software-spe- cific code within controlled execution boundaries rather than designing directly. The pilot implementations and industrial deployment demon- strate reliable conversational execution of representative engineering workflows across proprietary and OpenBIM environments, establishing the technical feasibility of the proposed architecture. The contribution is of interest to researchers and practitioners in construction informatics because it provides a reusable architectural pattern for human-AI collaboration that preserves deterministic engineering models while shifting human effort from software operation to communicating design. Future research should quantitatively evaluate productivity and usability, investigate scalability and multi-agent engineering workflows, and examine the broader implications of increasingly machine- rather than human-facing BIM.
title: Designing in English, not in Revit: an Agentic Architecture for BIM and Beyond
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Ontology-Based Engineering System for Knowledge-Driven Manufacturing of Customised Aerospace Parts
venue: IFIP advances in information and communication technology

abstract: Accurate cost estimation in the early stages of new product development (NPD) is increasingly challenged by the complexity of aerospace parts and the rapid expansion of manufacturing process knowledge. Traditional cost estimation approaches, often reliant on static models and expert judgment, struggle to adapt and integrate diverse, evolving process data. This paper introduces a novel Knowledge-Based System for Product Manufacturing Cost Estimation (KBS-PMCE) that leverages semantic technologies and natural language processing (NLP) to deliver explainable, extensible cost estimation capabilities. The proposed framework formalizes manufacturing knowledge into structured ontologies, enabling semantic interoperability and dynamic alignment of data sources, including the incorporation of newly defined manufacturing processes. Validation in a case study involving complex aerospace sheet metal (ASM) parts illustrates the framework’s potential to support cost estimation grounded in formalized process equations and reasoning logic. The results highlight the system’s potential to enhance decision-making and interoperability in smart manufacturing environments. Future research will aim to broaden the framework’s applicability across diverse manufacturing sectors and improve semantic alignment automation through the integration of large language models (LLMs).
title: Intelligent product manufacturing cost estimation framework driven by semantic technologies and knowledge-based systems
venue: International Journal of Computer Integrated Manufacturing

abstract: Enterprise application systems have defined how organisations operate for five decades. At their core, they are navigation systems. Users learn the system, find the transaction, fill the fields and execute. Intelligence exists at the margins. Execution remains human. This paper argues that a structural discontinuity is becoming visible. The emergence of agentic AI enables a fundamentally different paradigm in which intent is expressed and AI executes the necessary business processes across systems, without requiring users to navigate applications at all. We term this the Agentic Enterprise. This shift unfolds across three distinct layers. The first is the Intent-Based Interface, where the user expresses a goal and the system acts on it, assembling a dynamic workspace and executing the necessary transactions without requiring navigation. The second is Ubiquitous AI, where the system operates continuously without human initiation, sensing conditions, detecting anomalies and acting within its authorised scope before the user is aware that anything requires attention. The third is Imperceptible AI, where the system reads human behavioural signals and intervenes seamlessly within the user's existing workflow before the need is consciously formulated. Together these three layers describe the full trajectory from the enterprise that waits for human direction to the enterprise that operates continuously and governs itself. Their architectural consequence is that existing enterprise systems including ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning), CRM (Customer Relationship Management), PLM (Product Lifecycle Management), MES (Manufacturing Execution System) and HRMS (Human Resources Management System) do not disappear. They are abstracted beneath the agentic layers above them. The application layer becomes infrastructure. Intent becomes the interface. This paper proposes a reference architecture organised around four themes: Compose, Contextualise, Control and Converge. It positions the Orchestration Plane as the runtime engine that draws simultaneously from all four themes. It introduces the System of Engagement as the adaptive interface layer that assembles itself from orchestration outputs. It identifies cross-domain semantic interoperability as the principal unresolved architectural challenge. And it defines the engineering agenda required for enterprise-scale agentic systems including the physical AI layer that makes the Autonomous Enterprise possible for industrial enterprises.
title: From Navigation to Intent: Architecture of the Agentic Enterprise
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: This paper introduces a conceptual, architectural, and empirical framework for artificial intelligence (AI)-governed management of intelligent maturity in industrial ecosystems within the emerging paradigm of Industry 6.0. The study redefines the maturity concept, shifting from digital maturity – understood as the degree of technological integration – to intelligent maturity, interpreted as the capability of distributed systems to learn, adapt, and self-organize through human–AI co-evolution. Unlike existing digital maturity and AI readiness models, the proposed framework conceptualizes intelligent maturity as an integrated governance capability emerging from the interaction of technological, cognitive, organizational, and ecosystem dimensions. The analysis focuses on the national industrial ecosystem of the Russian Federation, comprising three core sectors: mining, manufacturing, and electricity, gas, and steam supply (including air conditioning). Empirical evaluation based on Rosstat data (2021–2023) demonstrates a steady growth of the Intelligent Maturity Index from 0.39 to 0.46, with the most dynamic increase observed in manufacturing (+0.07 points). This indicates a progressive transition of the industrial system from digital to intelligent maturity, reflected in increasing AI adoption, innovation activity, and adaptive capacity. A distributed cognitive architecture is proposed, comprising technological, cognitive, organizational, and ecosystem layers interconnected by AI-enabled feedback loops. Within this framework, AI functions as a co-governing cognitive agent, enabling reflexive decision-making, semantic interoperability, and predictive adaptation across distributed industrial networks. The research contributes to the theory and practice of intelligent management by positioning intelligent maturity as a measurable and actionable meta-category of Industry 6.0 governance that integrates technology, cognition, and ethics into a unified adaptive system.
title: AI-Governed Intelligent Maturity Management of Industrial Ecosystems in Industry 6.0
venue: AI Computer Science and Robotics Technology

abstract: This paper introduces an ontology system to support dynamic, explainable, and human-centric collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence-enabled non-human agents in cyber–physical environments. In this setting, Digital Twins (digital models of physical systems or processes that mirror their real-time state) and Human Digital Twins (digital representations of individual humans, including their physiological or cognitive states) may provide information to enable an appropriate dynamic allocation of the work that can be shared by humans and AI actors (i.e., sliding work sharing). A novel upper-level Sliding Work Sharing ontology is defined to support semantic interoperability and reasoning across diverse domains, facilitating sliding work sharing in complex environments. The ontology is grounded in Industry 5.0 concepts and built upon the Industrial Ontology Foundry core ontology. It extends conventional scheduling ontologies by incorporating key constructs for Digital Twins, Human Digital Twins, and dynamic task flows. We validate the ontology through two use cases from the domains of automation in construction and manufacturing. The collaborative construction case involves robots and humans, while the manufacturing one integrates legacy systems, artificial intelligence actors, and human planners. The developed ontology system is evaluated for its coverage and expressiveness through a novel Retrieval-Augmented Generation based methodology, applied on diverse Large Language Models to derive competency questions from external sources. This approach enhances conventional ontology validation techniques with a scalable and unbiased alternative. Logical consistency is confirmed using a range of standard reasoners. Our results demonstrate that the Sliding Work Sharing ontology has considerable flexibility and potential to advance human–AI teaming in future work environments. • Digital Twins and Sliding Work Sharing ontologies. • Large language model retrieval augmented generation for ontology evaluation. • Human AI-teaming in construction and manufacturing automation.
title: Enabling interoperable human–AI teaming for automation in construction and manufacturing via Digital Twins and Sliding Work Sharing ontologies

abstract: Abstract Recycling industries face distinct digitalization challenges compared to conventional manufacturing due to highly variable material inputs, heterogeneous and legacy equipment, frequent reconfiguration of process lines, and increasing regulatory and sustainability requirements. Although large volumes of operational data are generated across recycling plants, this data is often fragmented, inconsistently structured, and weakly contextualized, limiting reuse across manufacturing operations, analytics, and enterprise systems. The lack of shared semantics constitutes a major barrier to scalable digital transformation. This paper presents an architectural approach that addresses these challenges by implementing the ISA-95 (IEC 62264) equipment standard, implemented using a ThingWorx/Kepware technology stack. Kepware acts as the industrial connectivity and normalization layer, aggregating real-time data from control systems. ThingWorx consumes data from kepware and applies ISA-95 object models through reusable templates and information structures to represent assets, operational states, material flows, and performance indicators in a standardized manner across sites. This decouples data producers from data consumers and enables applications such as performance monitoring, material yield analysis, maintenance analytics, and regulatory reporting to be developed without additional point-to-point integrations. By grounding the data layer in ISA-95 semantics and operationalizing it through ThingWorx and Kepware, the proposed architecture enables semantic interoperability by design, supporting cross-site comparability, scalable analytics, and data-driven decision-making for sustainable digitalization in recycling industries. Furthermore, it enables Furter design of Agentic AI.
title: Implementing a Semantic Data Layer in Recycling Industry Towards Agentic AI
venue: IFIP advances in information and communication technology

abstract: The rapid emergence of autonomous AI agents is transforming artificial intelligence from isolated model inference into distributed systems of reasoning, communication, and action. This paper develops the vision of the Internet of Agentic AI (IoAI): an open ecosystem in which heterogeneous agents discover one another, negotiate responsibilities, exchange context, invoke tools, and execute workflows across cloud, edge, device, organizational, and cyber-physical environments. We synthesize foundations from single-agent agentic AI, multi-agent systems, distributed computing, communication networks, game theory, and security engineering to characterize the architectures and mechanisms required for scalable agent ecosystems. The paper examines agent deployment models, workflow lifecycles, communication protocols, interoperability layers, resource-management challenges, and trust architectures, with case studies in adaptive manufacturing and distributed operational coordination. The resulting framework highlights the central research challenges of controlled emergence, semantic interoperability, secure identity, incentive-compatible coordination, resource-aware orchestration, and governance for large-scale networks of autonomous agents.
title: The Internet of Agentic AI: Communication, Coordination, and Collective Intelligence at Scale

abstract: Within Industry 4.0, more applications include multi-agent systems and integrated software agents in the newly developed solutions, as they can provide a valuable contribution to the manufacturing processes. This makes it important to create a digital representation of those virtual assets, similar to how this is done for physical ones. The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) has been designed for just this purpose - to create models of assets, containing all the relevant information. Currently, this is standard for physical assets, however, it could be of value to extend it beyond. We propose the usage of the AAS for creating information models of software agents and suggest a generic approach to apply the AAS meta-model to ensure semantic interoperability between them. For this purpose, we outline a structure and a set of specific submodels to group agent attributes, which can provide a description of all relevant information for a given task. We provide two examples of concrete agents and outline how this approach will be further validated within future use cases.
title: Modelling Agents in Industry 4.0 Applications Using Asset Administration Shell
venue: International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART)

title: Ontology as the Semantic Foundation of Enterprise AI An Enterprise Semantic Architecture for Manufacturing Intelligence through a Comprehensive Review, Conceptual Framework, and Future Research Agenda

abstract: The Internet has evolved by progressively expanding what humanity connects: first computers, then people, and later billions of devices through the Internet of Things (IoT). While IoT succeeded in digitizing perception at scale, it also exposed fundamental limitations, including fragmentation, weak security, limited autonomy, and poor long-term sustainability. Today, advances in edge hardware, sensing, connectivity, and artificial intelligence enable a new phase: the Internet of Physical AI Agents. Unlike IoT devices that primarily sense and report, Physical AI Agents perceive, reason, and act in real time, operating autonomously and cooperatively across safety-critical domains such as disaster response, healthcare, industrial automation, and mobility. However, embedding fast-evolving AI capabilities into long-lived physical infrastructure introduces new architectural risks, particularly around interoperability, lifecycle management, and premature ossification. This article revisits lessons from IoT and Internet evolution, and articulates design principles for building resilient, evolvable, and trustworthy agentic systems. We present an architectural blueprint encompassing agentic identity, secure agent-to-agent communication, semantic interoperability, policy-governed runtimes, and observability-driven governance. We argue that treating evolution, trust, and interoperability as first-class requirements is essential to avoid hard-coding today's assumptions into tomorrow's intelligent infrastructure, and to prevent the high technical and economic cost of getting it wrong.
title: The Internet of Physical AI Agents: Interoperability, Longevity, and the Cost of Getting It Wrong
A Knowledge-Based Diagnostic Framework for Cross-Standard Conceptual Divergences in Industrial Reference Data

abstract: In future, demand response scenarios, a multitude of different types of resources are potentially to be used, e.g. electric vehicles, flexible residential loads and battery storage systems. In order to solve the problem of real-time communication of data among the various resources, it is likely to be using different communication protocols. An aggregator utilizing several types of resources is faced with a problem of semantic interoperability. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a testbed consisting of a microgrid model integrated with several controllers communicating with industrial grade protocols for demand response, including IEC 61850, OpenChargePoint protocol (OCPP), OpenADR and UDP.
title: Real-time Co-simulation Design of Micro-grid and Information Communication System Based on Multi-agent System
venue: Power System and Green Energy Conference (PSGEC)

abstract: The ACM Multimedia 2025 Industry Program presents a comprehensive overview of how multimodal AI is revolutionizing real-world applications. The program features contributions from over twenty industry leaders, covering a spectrum of domains from content creation and distribution to healthcare, manufacturing, and foundational technology. Keynotes by leaders from NEC and Google DeepMind address critical challenges in business transformation and media integrity, respectively. A dedicated seminar from Google explores advancements in video codecs like AV2 and the development of next-generation quality metrics using Large Language Models (LLMs). The program also includes twelve expert talks and seven demonstrations that showcase practical innovations, such as LLM-driven recommendation systems at Meta, generative AI for industrial optimization by Mitsubishi Electric, and a Siemens-developed protocol for semantic interoperability in manufacturing. These components collectively highlight the profound societal and industrial impact of multimedia research and bridge the gap between academic theory and real-world deployment.
title: An Innovative Industry Program on Multimedia in A New AI Era
venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

abstract: The powerful generative capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) has instigated a paradigm shift in recommendation. However, existing generative models (e.g., OneRec) operate as implicit predictors, critically lacking the capacity for explicit and controllable reasoning—a key advantage of LLMs. To bridge this gap, we propose OneRec-Think, a unified framework that seamlessly integrates dialogue, reasoning, and personalized recommendation. OneRec-Think incorporates: (1) Itemic Alignment: cross-modal Item-Textual Alignment for semantic grounding; (2) Reasoning Activation: Reasoning Scaffolding to activate LLM reasoning within the recommendation context; and (3) Reasoning Enhancement, where we design a recommendation-specific reward function that accounts for the multi-validity nature of user preferences. Experiments across public benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, our proposed "Think-Ahead" architecture enables effective industrial deployment, achieving a 0.159% gain in APP Stay Time and validating the practical efficacy of the model's explicit reasoning capability.
title: OneRec-Think: In-Text Reasoning for Generative Recommendation
Event-state knowledge graph-enhanced GraphRAG for order-driven 3D printing supply chain configuration

abstract: The exponential growth of data streaming from edge devices, IoT sensors, and transactional systems has rendered traditional Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) pipelines obsolete for real-time analytics. These conventional, rule-based pipelines struggle with dynamic workloads, unpredictable system failures, and the semantic heterogeneity of cross-industry data. This paper proposes a unified, AI-driven framework for optimizing real-time ETL pipelines deployed on cloud infrastructure. The framework integrates three core components: (1) a predictive auto-scaling engine utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to forecast workload volatility and dynamically allocate cloud resources, minimizing latency and cost; (2) a self-healing fault tolerance mechanism powered by reinforcement learning (RL) that proactively identifies anomalous node behaviour and orchestrates failover strategies without human intervention; and (3) a semantic interoperability layer employing graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models (LLMs) to map disparate data schemas (e.g., HL7 for healthcare, X12 for finance, and OPC-UA for manufacturing) into a unified, query-able format. We evaluate the proposed framework using a simulated multi-cloud environment with mixed-industry streaming datasets. Results demonstrate a 42% reduction in ETL latency during demand spikes, a 99.99% uptime through predictive self-healing, and a 95% reduction in manual schema-mapping efforts. This unified approach establishes a new paradigm for resilient, efficient, and interoperable real-time data processing across industry verticals.
title: AI-driven optimization of real-time ETL pipelines in cloud infrastructure: A unified framework for predictive scaling, fault tolerance and cross-industry data interoperability
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews

abstract: This thesis presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of Nora, an AI generative co-pilot developed to support the construction and refinement of bowtie diagrams in the field of industrial risk management. Bowtie diagrams are structured graphical models that illustrate how specific threats can lead to an undesired top event and, subsequently, to potential consequences, while also showing the preventive and mitigative barriers in place to control both threats and consequences. The work was conducted at Beawre Digital S.L., a technology start-up dedicated to digital risk automation and continuous risk management for the construction industry. Traditional bowtie tools are effective for visualization but require extensive manual effort, limiting knowledge reuse and scalability. Nora addresses these limitations by combining large language models (LLMs), embeddings, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) into a single interactive assistant that communicates through natural language and updates diagrams dynamically. The system was re-architected from a slow, error-prone prototype into a scalable, production-ready service. With this new approach, task or intent classification and context retrieval occur simultaneously, followed by real-time response streaming and persistent "smart view" storage in Azure Blob Storage. A multi-agent orchestration layer separates classification, generation, and validation tasks, ensuring linguistic consistency and robust recovery from errors. In parallel, a weighted embedding framework allows semantic comparison of bowtie diagrams, supporting knowledge reuse across projects. The entire pipeline is deployed securely through GitLab CI/CD, Docker, and Kubernetes for automated scalability. The empirical evaluation compared the improved and initial versions of Nora across three dimensions: correctness, latency, and cost. The results show significant improvements: mean latency decreased fivefold; correctness improved from 59% to over 93%; and cost per request was reduced by up to 70%. Statistical testing confirmed that these improvements were both reliable and significant. These advances stem from concurrent processing, structured and extensive prompt engineering, and asynchronous embedding computations. Conclusively, the thesis demonstrates that generative AI can operate reliably within structured industrial frameworks when supported by modular orchestration, validation, and semantic grounding. Nora thus represents a novel blend of conversational AI and formal safety methodologies that supports Beawre's vision of continuous, data-driven risk management. Future research will focus on multi-agent coordination, enhanced data governance, and the transition toward hosting and fine-tuning an in-house language model to ensure long-term independence and scalability.
title: Generative AI co-pilot for dynamic bowtie diagrams in construction risk management
venue: UPCommons institutional repository (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)

abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) integrates cyber-physical systems, edge-cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and advanced connectivity to enable intelligent, data-driven operations across manufacturing, energy, transportation, and healthcare. The convergence of Operational Technology (OT) and Information Technology (IT), together with pervasive AI-driven automation, complicates meeting the joint requirements of performance, adaptability, and security (PAS). This survey adopts an explicitly AI-centric view of PAS and reviews IIoT research spanning deep reinforcement learning (DRL), multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), digital twins (DTs), federated and collaborative learning, graph neural networks (GNNs), blockchain-assisted analytics, and lightweight and post-quantum cryptography. The reviewed approaches are analyzed across device, edge, fog, cloud, and application layers under industrial constraints such as latency, reliability, resource limits, safety requirements, and regulatory compliance. A PAS-centric taxonomy is introduced that links technique families to deployment layers and application domains, and recurring trade-offs among PAS dimensions are summarized. Open challenges are identified in multi-objective optimization, semantic interoperability, lifecycle validation, and governance, with directions outlined toward secure and sustainable Industry 5.0 IIoT ecosystems.
title: Performance, Adaptability, and Security in AI-Driven IIoT: A Survey
To Share or Not to Share: Orchestrating Trustworthy Data in Global Value Chains
Skill Modelling for Digital Factories
venue: IFIP advances in information and communication technology

abstract: Despite intensified recycling efforts, global material consumption has more than tripled over the past five decades, while the global circularity rate has declined. This widening gap reveals that incremental improvements are insufficient and that a transition toward circular economy must be structural. This transition is constrained by fragmented data ecosystems, limited transparency among stakeholders, and conventional digital twin architectures that struggle to represent the dynamic, multi-loop nature of circular supply networks. To address these challenges, this position paper discusses a conceptual Federated Digital Twin framework that integrates federated system architectures to protect data sovereignty, intelligent agents to enable real-time negotiation and synchronization, and knowledge graphs to ensure semantic interoperability across distributed actors. The framework serves as a decision-support backbone for circular manufacturing, aiming for a coordinated management and systemic coherence of value-retention strategies and production planning for circular supply chains.
title: Federated digital twins for intelligent decision-making in circular supply networks

abstract: Execution Governance 6.0 (EG6) proposes Governed Effect Grounding as a candidate research-architecture layer for consequential effect authorization. It addresses a specific operational question: when an authorization decision depends on claims about the external world, are those claims correctly and reconstructably bound to the exact referents, properties, sources or procedures, semantic mappings, temporal conditions, uncertainty treatment, and evidence dependencies on which the proposed effect actually depends? EG6 is cumulative rather than substitutive. It does not replace the Execution Governance Six Conditions, EG3 commitment integrity, EG4 fabric integrity, or EG5 regime integrity. Canonical Execution Governance already requires Live-Context Integrity and Sufficient Verifiable Proof. The candidate EG6 contribution is therefore narrower: making profile-relative, effect-dispositive grounding dependencies first-class, version-pinned, completeness-checked, commitment-bound, and independently reconstructable at effect commitment. The paper introduces six candidate Grounding Integrity properties: Referent Binding Integrity; Source & Procedure Integrity; Semantic Mapping Integrity; Temporal Applicability Integrity; Uncertainty-Bounded Interpretation; and Grounding Witness Closure. It also presents a candidate formal kernel, an incremental-obligation separability criterion, a synthetic referent-misbinding counterexample, a grounding-failure taxonomy, a minimal reference profile, machine-readable JSON artifacts, conformance and attack vectors, an EG5–EG6 handoff rule, and staged evidence gates for executable, formal, reproducible, and independently reconstructable validation. The prior-art boundary is deliberately explicit. EG6 does not claim invention of grounding, semantic grounding, provenance, attribute association, continuous authorization, sensor semantics, metrological traceability, data-quality vocabularies, context attestation, authorization evidence, or semantic interoperability. Instead, the research hypothesis is whether dependency-complete, effect-dispositive, commit-time grounding closure creates an independently falsifiable operational obligation not already fully specified by a named lower-layer implementation or profile. The architecture is intentionally cross-domain. Potential profiles include agentic AI, cyber-physical and autonomous systems, industrial control, payments and digital assets, healthcare, and public or institutional infrastructure. Version: Research Architecture v0.1.5Date: 30 August 2026Status: Independent research and pre-standardization candidate. This publication is not a standard, certification scheme, legal determination, production-safety assurance claim, proof of governance completeness, or novelty/patentability opinion.
title: Execution Governance 6.0: Governed Effect Grounding
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: Enterprise data analysis is emerging as a distinct frontier for autonomous agents. Compared with general-purpose interaction and software engineering, it operates in an open, ambiguous, and continuously evolving environment. These characteristics call for a data-agent architecture that treats semantics, methodology, execution, and evolution as first-class system concerns. To this end, we introduce QwenPaw-Data, an agentic data system designed for enterprise intelligent data analysis. QwenPaw-Data consolidates heterogeneous assets from warehouses, dashboards, documents, interaction logs, and historical tasks into reusable, governable, and evolvable analysis assets, then turns natural-language requests into end-to-end analytical workflows spanning data understanding, retrieval, analysis, report generation, and decision support. Its architecture decomposes the problem into three collaborative subsystems: DataBridge provides trustworthy semantic grounding through interconnected metadata, knowledge, and trace graphs; Skill-Hub codifies expert analytical methodology into reusable and verifiable skills; and Host materializes these evidence and method assets into controllable, artifact-centric runtime execution. Across these subsystems, semantics, methods, traces, and feedback are continuously deposited back into the system, forming a self-evolving asset flywheel. Experiments on public benchmarks and real-world industrial BI workloads show that QwenPaw-Data improves both verifiable data access capability and higher-level analytical quality, offering a practical foundation for reliable, traceable, and continuously improving enterprise data agents.
title: QwenPaw-Data: Bridging Facts, Methodology, and Execution for Autonomous Enterprise Data Analytics

abstract: The study is devoted to the analysis of the problems of coordination of interaction of subsystems in distributed automated production control systems (DAPCS). The work is aimed at finding effective methods and architectural solutions that ensure the coordinated functioning of territorially and functionally distributed components of the system in the context of dynamically changing production scenarios. The article provides a retrospective analysis of the evolution of approaches to organizing interaction in DAPCS, tracing the path from centralized monolithic architectures to modern flexible decentralized systems based on a service-oriented approach and multi-agent technologies. The key requirements for coordination mechanisms in DAPCS are systematized, including ensuring semantic interoperability, supporting dynamic reconfiguration of the link structure, taking into account real-time constraints, decentralized decision-making under uncertainty. The advantages and disadvantages of the basic architectural styles of interaction organization — canonical, event-oriented and service — are analyzed. Promising approaches to the construction of adaptive coordination mechanisms based on the multi-agent approach, the development of ontological models for representing knowledge about processes and resources, and the dynamic formation of coalitions of service agents for business process tasks are considered. A generalized conceptual model of a service-oriented multi-agent interaction coordination system is proposed, integrating the advantages of proactive decision making, semantic search and service composition. An experimental evaluation of the effectiveness of the proposed model is carried out using the example of solving the problems of coordinating customized assembly processes in flexible manufacturing systems. The results of the study show the promise of the combined use of the multi-agent approach and service-oriented architecture for building adaptive decentralized coordination mechanisms that ensure stable and effective interaction of RASUP components in a dynamic environment.
title: Coordination of interaction of subsystems in distributed automated production control systems
venue: Russian journal of resources conservation and recycling

abstract: (M2M) communication within Industry 4.0 environments. The growing adoption of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), cyber-physical systems (CPS), and intelligent software agents has enabled higher levels of industrial autonomy while introducing new governance challenges associated with security, trust, accountability, interoperability, transparency, and responsible autonomous decision-making. Following the PRISMA 2020 methodology, this review synthesizes peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2026 across multiple research domains, including industrial systems, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, semantic technologies, and information systems. The review examines existing governance approaches, the technologies that support them, implementation capabilities, persistent challenges, and areas requiring further investigation. The findings indicate that governance research is distributed across several interconnected domains, including AI governance, Industrial IoT governance, data governance, trust management, semantic interoperability, explainable AI, and cybersecurity. Although considerable progress has been achieved in areas such as authentication, access control, secure communication, semantic representation, and AI transparency, the available evidence remains fragmented. The review also identifies several recurring limitations, including limited validation in real industrial environments, the absence of standardized governance evaluation frameworks, restricted interoperability across heterogeneous systems, and insufficient accountability mechanisms for autonomous decision-making. Overall, the review shows that current research provides a solid basis for advancing governance in autonomous industrial environments. At the same time, it highlights the need for integrated governance frameworks, rigorous empirical validation in industrial settings, standardized evaluation methodologies, stronger interoperability, and more trustworthy governance mechanisms to support autonomous industrial systems. Keywords: Autonomous systems; Machine-to-machine communication; Industry 4.0; Industrial IoT; AI governance; data governance; explainable AI; knowledge graphs; trust management, and systematic literature review.
title: Governance Challenges in Autonomous Machine-to-Machine Communication: A Systematic Literature Review
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

abstract: This thesis investigates the development of Digital Twins (DTs), virtual representations of physical systems that support predictive monitoring, optimization, and lifecycle management. DTs rely on the integration of diverse software components, particularly Simulation Models (SiMs), yet current development practices face significant challenges in integrating, understanding, and orchestrating these heterogeneous elements. The research aims to address these challenges by applying Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) principles to facilitate the systematic, scalable, and robust development of DTs. Research Motivation and Framework The study begins by identifying the need for a more structured engineering approach to DT development. Although DTs are widely recognized as a key enabler for Industry 4.0, their implementation often relies on ad-hoc, domain-specific, and tool-dependent solutions. These fragmented practices hinder reuse, semantic interoperability, and cross-domain scalability. The research focuses on three dimensions of DTs: 1.Virtual Environment (VE) : representing the digital mirror of the physical system through executable models. 2.Digital Data : connecting and contextualizing information flows. 3.Services : enabling interaction and orchestration between components. The work is structured around five research questions (RQs) addressing (1) current practices, (2) tool support, (3) integration methods, (4) semantic interoperability, and (5) orchestration modeling. Empirical Research: DT Development Practices (RQ1)An empirical study involving 19 practitioners from academia and industry revealed diverse understandings of DTs but a shared agreement on their fundamental components: Physical Entity (PE), Virtual Entity (VE), data, connections, and purpose. The VE, composed mainly of SiMs, emerged as the most critical and complex element due to its executable and dynamic nature. Findings indicate a lack of standardized methodologies for integration and orchestration. Most practitioners develop custom or in-house tools, frequently adopting a multi-tool strategy combining several simulation and integration environments. While standards like FMI (Functional Mock-up Interface) are widely used, they often fail to support many required simulation engines. This underscores the need for flexible integration frameworks. Practitioners also highlighted issues of semantic interoperability, ensuring shared understanding across models, and SiM reusability, both linked to poor documentation and inconsistent metadata. Finally, orchestration practices were found to be domain-specific, lacking formalism and flexibility, motivating the need for a more systematic orchestration framework. Tooling Experimentation: Evaluating Open-Source Support (RQ2)The second part of the research assessed open-source (OS) tools for DT development, focusing on integration and orchestration support. A taxonomy of six essential features was developed to evaluate these tools objectively. This taxonomy provides a structured framework to assess capabilities such as interface generation, orchestration mechanisms, and semantic interoperability. Results showed that none of the evaluated tools (TwinOps, ThingsBoard, and Ptolemy II) fully supported all essential features. In particular:•Interface Generation was insufficiently supported, forcing developers to manually create interfaces for integrating heterogeneous SiMs.•Semantic Interoperability was poorly handled, with limited mechanisms for ensuring data consistency. •Orchestration capabilities were present but limited, especially for hybrid simulations combining different time semantics. These findings motivated the development of new MDE-based methods to fill these gaps. Model-Driven Support for Integration and Orchestration The thesis introduces three complementary model-driven methods designed to enhance DT development: 1. Interface Generation Method (Chapter 4, RQ3)A model-driven interface generation approach was proposed to simplify the functional integration of heterogeneous behavioral models. Three concepts were defined:•Common Interface (CI): an abstract interface independent of any simulation engine. •Model Interface Description (MID) and Formalism Interface Description (FID): model-specific descriptions supporting automated interface generation. These concepts standardize how SiMs communicate, enabling functional interoperability across different platforms and engines. The approach significantly reduces manual coding, promotes reuse, and ensures consistency in data exchange. 2. Metamodel for Simulation Model Comprehension (Chapter 5, RQ4)To address semantic interoperability and reusability, a metamodel-based approach was developed for systematically documenting SiMs. The metamodel captures metadata such as:•Data formats and units (for compatibility),•Scope and limitations (for substitutability),•Versioning and evolution history. This structure enables knowledge transfer, facilitates SiM reuse, and allows developers to detect semantic inconsistencies across components. The method includes a collaborative assimilation process aligned with natural cognitive workflows. Future extensions envision integrating semantic web technologies (e.g., RDF) and AI-driven assistants (LLMs) to automate documentation and evolution management. 3. OrchTwin and LOTTS: Language-Oriented Orchestration (Chapter 6, RQ5)The final contribution introduces OrchTwin, a language-oriented model-driven framework that formalizes DT orchestration. It is implemented in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL) called LOTTS (Language for Orchestrating Twin-based Systems).LOTTS allows defining orchestration workflows through four structured views: 1.Component Description 2.Communication Definition 3.Execution Specification4.Deployment Allocation It enables model-to-code transformations, automatically generating executable code from high-level orchestration models. LOTTS embeds metadata constraints (e.g., units, formats, validity checks), ensuring semantic consistency and improving integration between heterogeneous SiMs. The approach supports modular and iterative DT development, reducing implementation effort and increasing maintainability. Contributions to Digital Twin Engineering The thesis makes three major contributions: 1.A Taxonomy for Evaluating DT Tools A reproducible framework for assessing integration and orchestration capabilities in DT tooling, guiding future tool development and benchmarking. 2.Model-Driven Methods for DT Integration The combination of interface generation and metamodeling methods provides a systematic approach to achieving functional and semantic interoperability among heterogeneous components. 3.OrchTwin Framework and LOTTS DSLA complete orchestration solution that bridges the design–implementation gap through model-driven automation, offering scalability, reusability, and formal consistency across DT development phases. Collectively, these contributions demonstrate how MDE can address complexity in DT engineering, establishing formal connections between conceptual models and operational systems. Future Work The thesis identifies several promising research directions:•Extending the evaluation taxonomy to include consistency management and verification mechanisms. •AI-assisted development for automatic definition and interpretation of DT artifacts. •Automated reasoning in the metamodel to support SiM evolution and validation. •Expanding OrchTwin to integrate microservice-based architectures, enhancing modularity and scalability. •Large-scale industrial validation to test applicability across diverse domains. •Performance evaluation and optimization to improve scalability and adoption in production contexts. Conclusion This research provides a comprehensive methodological framework for Digital Twin development, emphasizing integration, semantic interoperability, and orchestration. By uniting empirical insights with model-driven techniques, the thesis contributes to the foundation of systematic, reusable, and automated DT engineering. The proposed approaches, interface generation, SiM metamodeling, and the OrchTwin framework, collectively advance the state of practice from ad-hoc development toward formalized and automated DT engineering. Through the integration of MDE principles, the thesis establishes a clear path toward scalable, consistent, and maintainable digital twin systems, paving the way for future research and industrial adoption.
title: A Model Orchestra in Digital Twins:A Model-Driven Approach to Integration and Orchestration

abstract: Industry 5.0 promotes human-centric production systems where humans and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) collaborate as partners rather than operating in isolated roles. In such contexts, semantic interoperability alone is insufficient, since successful collaboration requires not only a common interpretation of data, but also the alignment of situation awareness, mental models, intentions, and decision-making processes. In this context, this thesis investigates the transition towards cognitive interoperability in Cyber-Physical Enterprises (CPEs) by proposing a framework based on a Cognitive Digital Twin and a Cognitive Architecture to support human-CPS collaboration. The thesis first establishes a formal conceptualisation of cognitive systems and introduces a definition of cognitive interoperability that extends beyond semantic alignment. Based on cognitive psychology and team cognition theories, a Maturity Model of Cognitive Interoperability (MMCI) is proposed to characterise progressive levels of cognitive alignment, from shared situation awareness to joint decision-making with metacognitive regulation. The work then defines the notion of a Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) as a DT enriched with cognitive capabilities, and analyses the architectural requirements needed to operationalise cognition in such systems. To support structured reasoning and explainability, an ontology-based semantic foundation is designed to represent tasks, agents, capabilities, abilities, and contextual constraints within a unified knowledge model. In addition, the CLARION cognitive architecture is integrated as the decision-making core of the CDT, enabling hybrid neuro-symbolic operation by combining symbolic reasoning with learning mechanisms. The proposed framework is validated through an industrial human-robot collaborative assembly use case involving a UR5e cobot. Experimental results show that embedding cognition into the CDT improves adaptability, decision-making quality, and robustness in dynamic collaboration scenarios compared to a semantic-only baseline. Overall, this thesis provides conceptual foundations, modelling tools, and an implementable architecture to support the transition from semantic to cognitive interoperability in future human-centric manufacturing systems.
title: Vers l’interopérabilité cognitive : jumeau numérique cognitif et architecture cognitive pour la collaboration Humain-CPS

abstract: Intellectual property (IP) plays a crucial role in fostering innovation and economic growth. However, the complexity of IP rights and their legal frameworks across different jurisdictions poses challenges for standardization and interoperability. Ontologies have emerged as a powerful tool to address these challenges. This study, through a literature review, aims to identify and analyze existing ontologies in the IP domain, evaluating the predominance of researchers/groups, application contexts, legal frameworks, upper-level ontologies, conceptual coverage, representation languages, and adopted formalisms. The analysis reveals core conceptual elements, including IP rights, agents, events, conditions, agreements, and works of mind, which define the dynamics of IP life cycles. We identified a greater focus of the existing ontologies on Copyright when contrasted with aspects of Industrial Property. More ontologies addressed general legal frameworks rather than country-specific regulations. Additionally, the development of IP ontologies remains concentrated in a limited number of countries and research groups, indicating the need for broader collaboration. Many ontologies prioritize implementation aspects over conceptual clarity, potentially affecting interoperability. Despite these challenges, IP ontologies play a crucial role in supporting standardization, legal compliance, and data integration. The findings emphasize, among others, the importance of refining conceptual models, promoting harmonization to enhance semantic interoperability.
title: An Analysis of Ontologies for the Intellectual Property Domain

abstract: Business process models are widely used in enterprises to orchestrate workflows involving events, tasks, and agents. BPMN provides a standardized syntax to capture structural semantics, yet domain-level semantics often remain implicit, typically expressed through descriptive annotations. Thus, integrating BPMN processes with external data is challenging, limiting semantic interoperability. Building on the principles of Linked Data, several approaches have been proposed to embed BPMN processes within ontologies and knowledge graphs to overcome this limitation. However, current approaches are restricted to abstract process models, with limited or no support for dynamic runtime executions. Therefore, we introduce semantic BPMN (sBPMN), a framework for representing BPMN process models in a modular ontology directly derived from the official BPMN 2.0 XML schema, and their execution traces in a dynamic knowledge graph. Both static and dynamic fragments can then be easily linked to external sources. We demonstrate a system architecture compatible with state-of-the-art BPMN orchestration engines, showing that sBPMN enables semantic linking of process elements and external data as well as validation of process instances against formal constraints. Finally, we showcase the applicability of sBPMN in an industrial use case, where human–AI processes are modeled via BPMN and semantically enriched with domain data to facilitate standardization and semantic downstream analysis.
title: sBPMN: A Framework for Capturing Business Process Semantics in Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
venue: ACM International Conference on Knowledge Capture (K-CAP)

abstract: The integration of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) into Industry 4.0 ecosystems is severely hampered by a critical lack of interoperability. This challenge, stemming from diverse platforms, incompatible protocols, and heterogeneous data structures, creates a semantic gap that hinders collaboration between systems. To address this gap, this paper presents a semantic gateway that bridges the Asset Administration Shell (AAS) specification with the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) framework, enabling structured alignment of UAV telemetry data. Unlike existing static adapters, the proposed architecture provides a resilient, asynchronous pattern specifically optimized for the strict constraints of aerial robotics, including high-frequency telemetry, limited onboard computation, and intermittent network connectivity. The gateway’s effectiveness is rigorously evaluated through controlled benchmarks, high-fidelity software-in-the-loop (SITL) simulations, and edge hardware deployments. Results demonstrate that the configuration-driven transformation model maintains internal processing latency below 5 ms, making it transparent to primary flight-control loops, while preserving digital twin consistency during network disruptions without introducing state “ghosting” effects upon reconnection. The evaluation focuses on the semantic consistency of runtime data transformation rather than full cross-system semantic interoperability. Although demonstrated for UAVs, the gateway provides a generalizable architectural pattern for integrating other mobile ROS-based assets into Industry 4.0 ecosystems. This study offers a practical, validated approach to making robotic systems compatible with AAS, indicating potential reduction in industrial integration effort and enabling seamless multi-agent operations.
title: A Semantic Gateway for UAV Interoperability: Bridging ROS 2 and Asset Administration Shell
Research on the Process Equipment Industry Data Space Architecture and Intelligent Operation and Maintenance Mechanisms

abstract: This paper advances a paradigm shift in digital transformation discourse by treating technology not as a set of efficiency tools but as a structural force that actively reconfigures electronic appliance supply chains. Moving beyond incremental automation, it argues that digital enablers-IoT-driven real-time visibility, multi-agent AI for decentralized coordination, and synchronized digital twins-fundamentally reshape network topology, governance logic, and resilience architecture. Drawing on engineering management and industrial informatics, the study identifies three emergent structural archetypes: the Resilient Mesh, which replaces hierarchical control with protocol-based, federated autonomy; the Adaptive Spine, which strategically centralizes core capabilities while distributing peripheral functions to AI-optimized local clusters; and the Temporal Stack, which dynamically modulates supply chain configuration across product lifecycle phases to align with shifting priorities-from co-design intensity at launch to circularity integration in decline. The analysis reveals that implementation barriers are rarely technical but stem from deeper systemic tensions: semantic interoperability gaps between legacy ERP systems and IIoT event streams; governance conflicts between supplier data sovereignty and collective network intelligence; and critical shortages of professionals fluent in both supply chain dynamics and digital system semantics. Empirical grounding is strengthened through comparative functional mapping of AI coordination paradigms and governance delegation matrices, illustrating how decision authority, update frequency, and failure ownership vary across structural models. The paper concludes by proposing a theory of structurally-aware digital transformation, advocating for evaluation frameworks centered on structural impact metrics-such as node centrality redistribution and path redundancy-rather than conventional operational KPIs. It further outlines future research frontiers, including quantum-secure identity infrastructure, neuromorphic edge controllers for topology agility, and regulatory sandboxes enabling cross-border structural experimentation.
title: Digital Transformation and Structural Optimization of Electronic Appliance Supply Chains
venue: Journal of Electrotechnology Electrical Engineering and Management
